274.title: Sikhism: one creator
274.hook: the Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mool Mantar: one creator, truth is the name (Japji)
274.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib, which begins with the Mool Mantar, early each morning, and the Ik Onkar symbol appears over gurdwara doors, in homes and on the first page of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ramadan, the fasting month. Your line was hunger teaches. Today, a new visit: Sikhism.

The Sikh scripture begins with a number. Before a single word, on the very first page, there's the numeral one, written in Gurmukhi, the Punjabi script. You'll see that symbol everywhere in Sikh life: over the doors of gurdwaras, on car dashboards, on pendants, even tattooed on forearms. It comes before everything else the Gurus have to say. Today: Ik Onkar, and the few lines that follow it.
screen: `A HOLY BOOK THAT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.` → `OVER DOORS, ON DASHBOARDS.` → `IK ONKAR.`

segments.voice: Sikhism begins with Guru Nanak, born in Punjab, in what is now Pakistan. Sikh tradition says that as a young man he disappeared into a river for three days and came out with a message about one God, and spent the rest of his life traveling and singing it. His words, and those of the Gurus after him and of other saints, were gathered into the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru. It opens with the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Here is its sense, line by line; the Punjabi is compact, so this is a paraphrase. Ik Onkar: there is one creator, one being, present in everything. Sat Naam: whose name is truth. Karta Purakh: the creator. Nirbhau: without fear. Nirvair: without hate. Akal Murat: beyond time. Ajuni: never born. Saibhang: existing by itself. Gur Prasad: known by the Guru's grace. Nine short phrases, and a whole picture of God. Ik is the numeral one, written as a digit, not spelled out; some readers see in that a way of leaving no room for doubt. Onkar is a name for the one reality, and some read the long curving line drawn over the top as that oneness reaching on without end. Sikhs say this one creator isn't far off: the same one is in every person, which is why Sikh teaching insists on the equality of all people, whatever their caste, gender or faith. The Mool Mantar opens Japji Sahib, the prayer Sikhs who keep the daily prayers recite each morning.
screen: `GURU NANAK, PUNJAB.` · `THE MOOL MANTAR: THE ROOT VERSE.` · `WITHOUT FEAR, WITHOUT HATE.` · `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Draw the numeral one slowly, with a pen on a scrap of paper or with your finger on your palm, and breathe out as you draw, letting the word one settle in you. Then picture the people you'll see today, one by one, and hold the thought that the same one is in each of them.
Ik Onkar. One creator: the numeral one that opens the Sikh scripture, the first words of the Mool Mantar. Today's word.
Your line: one. One creator, and the same one in everyone. That's two hundred seventy-four days.

275.title: Sikhism: remembering the name
275.hook: remembering God through the name, in breath and song
275.howItsDone: Many Sikhs rise at amrit vela before dawn to recite Japji and meditate on Waheguru, join kirtan in the gurdwara, and repeat the name quietly through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ik Onkar, the numeral one that opens the Sikh scripture. Your line was one.

Long before sunrise in Amritsar, the city is dark, but the Golden Temple is lit up, its reflection shivering on the water around it. People are already walking the marble path barefoot, and from inside comes music: a harmonium, small drums, voices singing verses from the scripture. It goes on, in shifts, almost all day. Some of the walkers sing along. Some are silent, lips barely moving, repeating a single word.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE IN AMRITSAR.` → `MUSIC FROM INSIDE THE TEMPLE.` → `ONE WORD, LIPS BARELY MOVING.`

segments.voice: Naam means the name. In Sikh teaching it's more than a label: it's the presence of the one creator, yesterday's Ik Onkar, running through everything. Simran means remembering. So naam simran is remembering the name, keeping the one close until the mind is steeped in it. Sikh tradition counts it the first of three pillars of Sikh life, taught by Guru Nanak; the other two, honest work and sharing, come in the next two days. How is it done? Sikhs often repeat Waheguru, a Sikh name for God often explained as wonderful Lord, or wondrous teacher, silently or aloud, sometimes with the breath: wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath. Some rise in the hours before dawn, called amrit vela, the ambrosial time, to bathe, recite Japji and sit in simran before the day starts. And much of it is sung. The Guru Granth Sahib is written almost entirely as poetry set to musical modes called raags, and kirtan, singing it, fills the gurdwara. A line in the Sukhmani Sahib, by the fifth Guru, Arjan, says in effect: remember, remember, remember, and find peace. The Gurus taught this wasn't escape from the world. Guru Nanak compared a person living with the name to a lotus that grows in muddy water yet isn't stained by it. The idea is to keep the name while living a full, busy life, not instead of one.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME, THE PRESENCE.` · `SIMRAN — REMEMBERING.` · `WAHEGURU, WITH THE BREATH.` · `A LOTUS IN MUDDY WATER.` · then, large: `THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Borrowed from kirtan: breathe in, and on the out-breath let one low, easy note hum in your chest. If you're Sikh, you might let Waheguru ride on the note; if not, the hum alone is enough, or any word that points you toward what matters. When thoughts come, let them float like the lotus on the water, and come back to the sound.
Naam simran. Remembering the name: keeping the one creator in mind, in breath and song, through a busy day. Today's word.
Your line: the name. In breath, in song, in the hours before dawn. See you tomorrow.

276.title: Sikhism: honest work
276.howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to earn their living through honest work in any trade or profession, avoiding exploitation and begging, and to keep remembering the name while they work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: naam simran, remembering the name in breath and song. Your line was the name.

A holy man comes to town. Two invitations arrive. One is from the richest official in the district, throwing a lavish feast in his honor. The other is from a poor carpenter with only coarse bread to offer. Which would you accept? The feast has the better food, the better company, the better look. The holy man was Guru Nanak, and he went to the carpenter's.
screen: `TWO INVITATIONS.` → `A FEAST, OR COARSE BREAD?` → `HE WENT TO THE CARPENTER'S.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the janamsakhis, the traditional life stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs tell it often. The carpenter was Bhai Lalo. The rich man, Malik Bhago, was offended and demanded to know why the Guru had refused his feast. So, the story goes, Guru Nanak took Lalo's dry bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezed. From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's came blood. One had been earned by honest labor; the other squeezed out of the poor. That's the heart of kirat karni: earning your living by honest work. Kirat means work, labor; karni means doing. It's the second of the three pillars Guru Nanak taught, after remembering the name. And it pushes against a familiar picture of holiness: leaving work behind to live on alms. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1245, he criticizes those who call themselves holy while begging at other people's doors, and praises the one who eats what he earns by his own effort and gives some away. That person, he says, recognizes the path. Sikh tradition says he lived it: in the last years of his life he settled at Kartarpur, on the bank of the Ravi, and farmed, working the fields alongside the community. For Sikhs, honest work isn't a distraction from the spiritual life; it's part of it. No cheating, no exploiting, no living off others when you can work, and the name remembered while the hands are busy.
screen: `BHAI LALO AND MALIK BHAGO.` · `MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.` · `EAT WHAT YOU EARN.` · `THE GURU FARMED AT KARTARPUR.` · then, large: `HONEST WORK.`

segments.voice: Picture the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid: a job, a class, a household, caring for someone. Ask quietly whether you're cutting a corner, bending the truth, taking credit, or leaning on someone else's effort; no guilt, just notice. Then choose one piece of it to do fully and cleanly.
Kirat karni. Earning your living by honest work: the second pillar of Sikh life, lived by Guru Nanak in the fields at Kartarpur. Today's word.
Your line: honest work. Bread like Lalo's, earned with your own hands. Day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: Sikhism: share
277.hook: share what you earn with others
277.howItsDone: Many Sikhs set aside dasvandh, a tenth of their income, for the community and those in need, and give time as seva in the gurdwara, from cleaning to cooking for the shared meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirat karni, and the carpenter's bread. Your line was honest work.

A father gives his teenage son twenty rupees, a real sum, and sends him to the market with one instruction: make a good deal. Buy something you can sell for a profit. Learn the family business. On the road the boy meets a group of holy men who haven't eaten in days. He spends every rupee on food for them, and comes home empty-handed. His father is furious. The boy is calm: he made the truest deal there is. The boy was the young Nanak.
screen: `TWENTY RUPEES AND ONE INSTRUCTION.` → `HUNGRY MEN ON THE ROAD.` → `THE TRUEST DEAL.`

segments.voice: That story, like yesterday's, comes from the janamsakhis, and Sikhs call it sacha sauda, the true bargain. A gurdwara stands today where tradition says it happened. It's a picture of the third pillar of Sikh life: vand chhakna, to share and consume together. Vand means dividing, sharing out. Chhakna means eating, partaking. Share what you have, then enjoy it, together. The three pillars fit: remember the name, earn honestly, share what you earn. Yesterday's hymn at Ang 1245 holds the last two in one breath: the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path. Honest work without sharing can turn into hoarding. Sharing without honest work isn't really yours to give. Sikhs made this concrete. Sikh tradition asks for dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of one's income for the community and those in need, a practice that grew under the later Gurus. Sharing also means time and skill, not only money. Sikhs call selfless service seva, and you'll see it in any gurdwara: people cleaning shoes, sweeping floors, chopping onions, who may spend the rest of the week as doctors, drivers or shopkeepers. A kitchen where everyone eats together is tomorrow's story. Underneath it all, everything comes from the one creator of three days ago, so nothing is entirely private property. Sharing isn't charity from above. It's handing around what was always meant to go around.
screen: `SACHA SAUDA — THE TRUE BARGAIN.` · `VAND — SHARE. CHHAKNA — PARTAKE.` · `EARN, THEN GIVE SOME AWAY.` · `DASVANDH — A TENTH.` · then, large: `SHARE IT.`

segments.voice: Think of what you'll eat today, and who you could share it with: a coworker at lunch, a neighbor, a friend who's struggling, a stranger outside the shop. Picture handing it over, and eating together if you can. Notice any reluctance, and let it soften.
Vand chhakna. Share and partake: the third pillar of Sikh life, giving some of what you honestly earn. Today's word.
Your line: share it. Earned honestly, then handed around. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: Sikhism: the free kitchen
278.hook: in every gurdwara, anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor as equals
278.howItsDone: Gurdwaras keep a langar where volunteers cook and serve a free vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chhakna, sharing what you earn. Your line was share it.

A long hall, a clean floor, long strips of cloth laid down in rows. A student sits down. Next to her, a taxi driver still in his work jacket. Then a grandmother, a tourist with a backpack, a man who hasn't eaten since yesterday. Volunteers walk the rows with buckets and ladles: lentils, a vegetable curry, warm flatbread dropped into open hands. Nobody asks your name, your religion or whether you can pay. Nobody gets a better seat. This is the free kitchen, and the idea of sitting together.
screen: `A LONG HALL, ROWS ON THE FLOOR.` → `NO NAMES, NO BILL, NO BETTER SEAT.` → `THE FREE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The word is langar: the community kitchen that belongs to every gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, and also the meal served there. Sikh tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru. It grew under the second Guru, Guru Angad, and Sikhs especially remember his wife, Mata Khivi, who ran the kitchen and made sure the food was generous. Sikh tradition remembers why it mattered. In that world, who could eat with whom was bound up with caste, and eating side by side crossed lines people had been raised not to cross. The third Guru, Guru Amar Das, made it a rule, remembered in a short Punjabi phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First sit in the row, then join the gathering. A story Sikhs tell says even the Mughal emperor Akbar, coming to see the Guru, first sat on the floor and ate in the row like everyone else. The historical details of that visit are debated, but the point of the story isn't. The food is simple and vegetarian, so people of almost any diet or faith can eat it. Volunteers cook and serve it as seva, selfless service. And it runs at every scale, from a small gurdwara's kitchen to the vast langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where still nobody pays. So langar holds two lessons. Yesterday's: share what you have. Today's: when you share, sit at the same level. Nobody above, nobody below. Everyone sits together.
screen: `LANGAR — THE COMMUNITY KITCHEN.` · `GURU NANAK, GURU ANGAD, MATA KHIVI.` · `FIRST SIT IN THE ROW.` · `SIMPLE FOOD, SERVED AS SEVA.` · then, large: `EVERYONE SITS TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Picture a row on a floor, and put yourself in it. Fill the places beside you: someone you love, someone you pass every day and never speak to, someone you find hard, all at the same height, with the same plate. Notice where that's easy and where it pinches.
Langar. The free community kitchen of the gurdwara, and the meal shared there, where everyone eats at the same level. Today's word.
Your line: everyone sits together. Same floor, same plate, nobody above. Day two hundred seventy-eight, done.

279.title: Sikhism: rising spirits
279.hook: Sikhs speak of staying in high spirits, even in hard times
279.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala in everyday conversation and close the daily Ardas with a line asking for rising spirits through the Name and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday: langar, the free kitchen where everyone eats at the same level. Your line was everyone sits together.

You ask someone how they're doing. Their week has been rough, and you know it: a lost job, a sick parent, a flood in the basement. They smile and say something that isn't denial and isn't a brave act either. Something like: it's hard, and we're in good spirits. You can hear they mean both halves. Sikhs have a phrase for that second half, chardi kala, and it isn't a mood you wait for. It's a way of standing.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU DOING?` → `IT'S HARD, AND WE'RE IN GOOD SPIRITS.` → `CHARDI KALA.`

segments.voice: Chardi kala is Punjabi. Chardi means rising, climbing, going up. Kala is harder to put in one English word: spirit, energy, strength, a state of being. Together: rising spirits, or ever-ascending spirit. You'll hear it in ordinary talk, on banners, at the end of messages. And it comes in the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing, near the close of worship. Near its end comes a line that runs, roughly: Nanak, through the Name may our spirits rise, and by your will may there be good for all. Notice the pairing: rising spirits, and the good of everyone. Not just my spirits. It matters that Sikhs, of all people, say this. The Ardas also remembers hard history: Gurus and ordinary Sikhs who were imprisoned, tortured and killed rather than give up their faith. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was executed in Lahore. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth, was beheaded in Delhi. So chardi kala was never a slogan for easy days. It was learned in the worst ones. And it isn't pretending. Those who speak of it say grief and anger are real; chardi kala is where you stand while you feel them. It rests on trust in the Creator's will, which Sikhs call hukam, and on remembering the Name, the practice from four days ago. The spirit rises because it's tied to something that doesn't sink. For anyone on any path, it offers a question for a bad day: not how do I feel nothing, but where do I stand?
screen: `CHARDI — RISING. KALA — SPIRIT.` · `SAID DAILY IN THE ARDAS.` · `LEARNED IN THE HARDEST DAYS.` · `NOT PRETENDING, STANDING.` · then, large: `RISING SPIRITS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one setback that's with you this week, small or large, and let it be as heavy as it is. On the next breath in, feel your spine lengthen a little, as if something lifts from the crown of your head. The weight is still there; you're just standing a bit taller under it.
Chardi kala. Rising spirits: steady, hopeful strength that holds even in hard times, rooted in trust. Today's word.
Your line: rising spirits. Hard days are real, and so is where you stand. See you tomorrow.

280.title: Vaisakhi, the harvest
280.hook: the spring harvest festival, and the founding of the Khalsa in 1699
280.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi with worship at the gurdwara, processions called nagar kirtan, langar, and often amrit initiation ceremonies; in Punjab it is also a harvest celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala, spirits that rise even in hard times. Your line was rising spirits.

Mid-April in Punjab. The wheat has turned gold and it's time to cut it. Farmers have waited all winter, and when the harvest comes in there's drumming, dancing, the big swinging steps of bhangra. Communities across north India keep this harvest festival. But for Sikhs, the same day carries a second story, one that changed the shape of their whole community on a single morning in 1699. On the last day of this visit to Sikhism: Vaisakhi.
screen: `MID-APRIL, THE WHEAT TURNS GOLD.` → `A HARVEST, AND A SECOND STORY.` → `VAISAKHI.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi takes its name from Vaisakh, a month in the Indian calendar, and it falls in mid-April. Here's the story Sikhs tell. In 1699 the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, called Sikhs to gather at Anandpur. Before the crowd he drew a sword and asked: who will give his head for the faith? Silence. Then one man stood up. The Guru led him into a tent and came out alone, the sword wet. He asked again. Another stood. Five times. Tellings differ about what happened inside the tent, but they agree on the ending: the five came out alive, dressed in new clothes. Sikhs call them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. They came from different castes and different regions, and that mattered deeply. The Guru stirred water and sugar in an iron bowl with a double-edged sword, and tradition says his wife added the sweetness. With this amrit he initiated the five into the Khalsa, a community of committed Sikhs, and gave the men the name Singh, lion. Women who take amrit are named Kaur, often rendered princess. Then the surprise. The Guru knelt and asked the five to initiate him. The teacher became a student of his own students. Put the two stories together, the harvest and the Khalsa, and you get a festival about beginnings: a field that starts over, and a community that started over. A good end to a week that began with one creator, then the name, honest work, sharing, the kitchen and rising spirits.
screen: `VAISAKH — A MONTH, MID-APRIL.` · `ANANDPUR, 1699: WHO WILL STAND?` · `THE FIVE BELOVED ONES.` · `THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE TO INITIATE HIM.` · then, large: `A NEW BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your life that is starting over, or could: a job, a friendship after a gap, a habit, a morning. Hold it the way a farmer looks at a field after the harvest: cleared, open, ready. Breathe in and let it be new; breathe out and let last season go.
Vaisakhi. The April harvest festival, and for Sikhs the day the Khalsa was founded in 1699. Today's word.
Your line: a new beginning. That's the week with Sikhism, from one creator to rising spirits. Tomorrow, home.
